strengths: The core idea of combining multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) with Stein-based control functionals (CF) is intuitive and well-motivated, addressing settings where integrands are expensive to evaluate at high fidelity and target densities are known only up to a normalizing constant.
Unlike Multilevel Bayesian Quadrature, which typically requires closed-form kernel integrals under specific priors, Stein-based control functionals can handle unnormalized posterior distributions.

Preliminary empirical results on the boundary-value ODE and Lotka-Volterra Bayesian inference tasks demonstrate empirical variance reduction compared to standard MLMC and single-level CF under fixed computational budgets.
weaknesses: The methodological and theoretical novelty is quite incremental. Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 are direct, straightforward extensions of existing control functional results (Oates et al., 2017; 2019) applied independently to each level of a standard telescoping sum.

A fundamental pillar of Multilevel Monte Carlo is optimal sample allocation across levels based on the decay of variance and cost. The paper does not derive or analyze the optimal allocation for MLCF (where level variances decay at faster kernel rates), and instead simply uses the standard MLMC sample sizes. The authors acknowledge this gap in Section 5 ('In this initial work... In the full version of this paper we will consider the optimal sample size at each level of MLCF'), indicating the manuscript is an incomplete work or extended abstract not yet ready for a full conference paper.

The empirical evaluation is very limited, covering only two low-to-moderate dimensional synthetic/benchmark tasks (a 2D ODE and an 8D ODE system) with only three budget points. Comparisons against other modern variance reduction baselines or multifidelity methods are missing.

The computational overhead of computing Stein kernels (evaluating score functions $\nabla \log \pi$) and inverting kernel matrices ($O(n^3)$) is largely brushed aside with the claim that evaluating $f$ dominates. A thorough wall-clock time breakdown and scaling study with respect to sample size $n_l$ and dimension $d$ are needed.
Presentation and proofreading issues are present: for instance, both Table 1 and Table 2 have repeated column headers ('l = 0 | l = 1 | l = 1') instead of listing level $l = 2$.

strengths: The idea of combining Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) with Stein-based control functionals (CF) is intuitive and well-motivated for expensive numerical models where unnormalized posterior densities arise.
The proposed method is versatile enough to be applied to problems with unnormalized densities without requiring problem-specific hand-crafted control variates.
Initial empirical results on the boundary-value ODE and the Lotka-Volterra system show encouraging variance reduction over standard MLMC and standard CF under fixed time budgets.
weaknesses: Limited technical and theoretical novelty: The methodology directly applies the existing Stein control functional framework (Oates et al., 2017; 2019) to the increments in the standard MLMC telescoping sum. Theorem 2 is a direct application of the error bound from Oates et al. (2019) summed over independent levels, offering limited new theoretical insight.

Incomplete methodology regarding optimal sample allocation: A foundational component of MLMC methods is the optimal allocation of samples ($n_l, m_l$) across levels balancing variance reduction against computational cost. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the conclusion ('In this initial work... In the full version of this paper we will consider the optimal sample size at each level of MLCF'), and in the experiments they simply plug in the sample allocations optimized for standard MLMC rather than for MLCF.

Experimental setup is unclear and very limited: In Tables 1 and 2, the sample size at the finest level ($l=2$) is extremely small ($n_l \in \{2, 4, 5, 6\}$). It is not clearly explained how the dataset was split into $m_l$ (for learning the CF) and $n_l - m_l$ (for evaluation) when $n_l = 2$. Standard work-precision plots (log-log plots of RMSE vs. wall-clock time) typical of the MLMC literature are missing, showing only boxplots at three arbitrary budgets.

Clarity and presentation issues: Tables 1 and 2 repeat '$l=1$' twice in the header instead of '$l=2$'; in the definition of $k_0(x, x')$ on page 2, the third term has $\nabla_x k(x, y)$ instead of $\nabla_x k(x, x')$; in Proposition 1, the sample index in the bracket erroneously reads $x_{(l-1,i)}$ instead of $x_{(l,i)}$; and there are typos such as 'Baysian' in Section 1.

strengths: Combining Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) with Stein-based control functionals is conceptually sound and provides a natural way to reduce variance in multifidelity integration problems with unnormalized posteriors.
The theoretical variance bound (Theorem 2) clearly outlines the convergence behavior and indicates the rate improvement under appropriate smoothness assumptions.

The empirical results on the boundary-value ODE and the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model show promising variance reduction compared to standard MLMC and standard control functionals under fixed computational budgets.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The proposed method essentially applies existing Stein control functionals (Oates et al., 2017; 2019) separately to each term in the standard MLMC telescoping sum. The proof of Theorem 2 is a direct level-wise application of the existing bound from Oates et al. (2019).

The paper is self-described as preliminary work. In Section 5, the authors write: 'In this initial work we introduced... In the full version of this paper we will consider the optimal sample size at each level of MLCF', indicating that critical components (such as optimal sample and budget allocation across levels for MLCF) are missing from this submission.

The empirical evaluation is quite limited, consisting of only two small toy problems (d=2 and d=8). Given the known vulnerability of kernel Stein methods to the curse of dimensionality (as seen in the $m^{-	au_l/d}$ rate), a more comprehensive evaluation on higher-dimensional problems is needed.

There are presentation and clarity issues throughout the paper. For instance, in both Table 1 and Table 2, the level headers are erroneously printed as '$l=0$, $l=1$, $l=1$' instead of '$l=0$, $l=1$, $l=2$'. Furthermore, it is not sufficiently explicit whether the experiments employ the unbiased estimator from Proposition 1 or the biased simplified estimator from Remark 1, nor how $m_l$ is chosen relative to $n_l$.

strengths: The paper presents a natural, well-motivated integration of Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) with non-parametric Stein-based control functionals (CFs), addressing the variance of level differences in multi-fidelity settings.

Theoretical analysis is thorough: Theorem 3.2 establishes explicit variance upper bounds inheriting the faster convergence rates of CFs, and Theorem 3.3 derives the optimal sample allocation across levels under computational budget constraints.
The extension to variational inference (Proposition 3.4) provides a recursive formulation that mitigates the memory and computational burden across optimization iterations.

The empirical evaluation is diverse and well-structured, spanning synthetic benchmarks, boundary-value ODEs, unnormalized posterior inference for the Lotka-Volterra system, and Bayesian neural networks.
weaknesses: The conceptual and technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the methodology largely amounts to plugging standard Stein control functionals (Oates et al., 2017/2019) into each term of the MLMC telescoping sum, and the proof techniques directly adapt existing results from Wendland (2004) and Oates et al. (2019).

In the Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) experiments, performance is plotted against training iterations rather than wall-clock time or total computational budget. Computing Stein kernels and score functions adds per-iteration overhead; evaluating solely by iteration count gives an incomplete picture of computational efficiency.

Unclear behavior of CF in the BNN experiment with sample size $n=1$: Appendix D.5 states that MLCFRG uses only 1 sample. Under the standard simplified CF estimator (Eq. 11), a single sample $n=1$ leads to trivial cancellation where the estimator simply returns $f(x_1)$ without any variance reduction. The paper should explicitly clarify how CF is applied in this setting.

The theoretical bounds suffer from an explicit curse of dimensionality through the exponent $	au/d$. While the paper acknowledges this in the text, applying the method to parameter spaces with $d \approx 400	ext{--}500$ (as in the BNN experiments) diverges significantly from the theoretical regime where convergence rate gains are guaranteed.
Minor grammatical and typographic errors are present (e.g., 'Theorem 3.2,its variance', 'a simplier form', 'in in Appendix D.1', and 'as we shown').

strengths: Combining multi-fidelity Monte Carlo (MLMC) with non-parametric Stein-based control functionals (CFs) is a natural and well-motivated concept for variance reduction in multi-fidelity scientific computing.
The paper is clearly written, logically structured, and provides explicit derivations for the optimal sample allocation across levels under a total computational budget constraint (Theorem 3.3).

The empirical evaluation covers several relevant problem domains, including differential equations (ODE boundary-value problem) and Bayesian parameter estimation (Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system).
weaknesses: Fundamental technical issue in the Variational Inference (MLCFRG) experiments: In Section 4 and Appendix D.5, the authors evaluate MLCFRG using a sample size of n = 1. However, for a single sample (n = 1), the control functional estimator in Equation (11) evaluates to 1^T k_0(X,X)^{-1} g(X) / (1^T k_0(X,X)^{-1} 1) = g(x_1) / 1 = g(x_1), where the Stein kernel and its inverse cancel out identically. As a result, the Stein control functional vanishes and does no variance reduction at all. Despite this, the paper includes a subsection titled 'Extra Experiments: Effect of Kernels' claiming to study kernel choices with n = 1, which is mathematically impossible given the cancellation. The reported gains in Figures 5–9 are therefore artifacts of the recursive update rather than the proposed control functionals.

Flawed variance claim in Proposition 3.4: In Appendix B.5, the authors bound the variance of the gradient estimator by conditioning on (lambda_L - lambda_{L-1}) and treating it as deterministic, claiming the variance depends only on the L-th increment. This is mathematically invalid because lambda_L is an accumulated random variable that depends on all preceding stochastic gradient steps; the true variance of the estimator accumulates the variances of all levels l = 0, ..., L.

Inconsistency between theory and implementation for VI: Proposition 3.4 is derived strictly for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), where lambda_{L+1} - lambda_L = -alpha_L nabla L. However, in Appendix D.5, the authors state that Adam is used. The non-linear moment calculations of Adam cannot be telescoped or rewritten into the 1-step recurrence of Equation (9).

Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 3.1 is an immediate consequence of the zero-mean property of Stein operators. Theorem 3.2 is a direct application of the bound from Oates et al. (2019) to independent increments across levels. Theorem 3.3 follows standard Lagrange multiplier optimization analogous to Giles (2008, 2015) with the CF rate substituted for the MC rate.

Curse of dimensionality: The theoretical error rate scales as O(m^{-tau/d}). In higher dimensions (e.g., d = 8 in Lotka-Volterra, or d = 392/522 in the BNN experiment), non-parametric Stein kernels suffer severely from the curse of dimensionality. For instance, at level 2 of the Lotka-Volterra experiment, only n_2 = 2 samples are used in an 8-dimensional space, where kernel interpolation provides little to no meaningful variance reduction.

strengths: Well-motivated concept: Combining non-parametric Stein-based control variates (control functionals) with the multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) framework addresses a real computational bottleneck when evaluating expensive simulation models and numerical integrands.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The paper establishes variance upper bounds for the MLCF estimator under scattered data approximation assumptions (Theorem 3.2) and derives the closed-form optimal sample size allocation across fidelity levels under a fixed budget constraint (Theorem 3.3).

Novel extension to Variational Inference: Proposition 3.4 provides an efficient recursive formulation (MLCFRG) for stochastic gradient updates, successfully linking multilevel control variates with reparameterized gradient estimation.

Diverse experimental validation: The method is validated across forward uncertainty quantification (PDE/ODE problems), Bayesian posterior inference with unnormalized densities using MCMC samples (Lotka-Volterra), and Bayesian neural network optimization.
weaknesses: Discrepancy between theory and high-dimensional experiments: The theoretical variance bound exhibits the typical curse of dimensionality through the exponent $m_l^{-	au_l / d}$, indicating that theoretical gains are limited to small or moderate dimensions. However, Section 4 applies the method to Bayesian neural networks with $d = 392$ and $d = 522$ without sufficient theoretical explanation or ablation of why Stein-based CFs remain effective in this regime.

Unclear experimental details and overhead in Variational Inference: For the BNN experiments (Figures 5 and 6), performance is plotted against optimization iterations rather than wall-clock time. Since computing Stein kernel derivatives and solving linear systems adds per-step overhead, iteration-based comparisons may mask the actual computational trade-offs.

Ambiguity in sample size allocation for VI: Appendix D.5 states that MLCFRG uses only 1 sample while baselines use 5 samples. It is unclear how a Stein control functional (which requires partitioning into $m$ interpolation points and $n-m$ evaluation points, or at least inverting a kernel matrix) is constructed with a single sample.

Lack of wall-clock runtime ablations for the kernel Gram matrix: Inverting kernel Gram matrices costs $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$. While coarse levels often require larger sample allocations ($m_0$), the paper does not systematically report the end-to-end wall-clock time overhead introduced by the kernel computations relative to standard MLMC.
